hook.text: Your phone connects to a satellite directly — no dish, no special antenna. Just your smartphone.

buildup.text: 3GPP is standardizing phone-to-satellite links. SOS via satellite already works on iPhones.

discovery.text: AST SpaceMobile and T-Mobile test broadband from space to unmodified phones. No dead zones.

twist.text: Bandwidth per satellite is limited. Millions of phones at once overwhelm it. Supplemental only.

climax.text: Non-terrestrial networks include drones and balloons too. Google Loon proved the concept.

punchline.text: Phones connecting to satellites. Universal coverage is becoming real.

quiz.question: What is the current main use case for direct-to-satellite phone connectivity?
options: Emergency SOS messages from areas with no cell coverage
Streaming 4K video from anywhere on Earth

details.summary: Non-terrestrial networks integrate satellites, high-altitude platforms, and drones into cellular network architecture. 3GPP standards for NTN extend 5G coverage to areas without terrestrial towers, enabling global connectivity for aviation, maritime, and remote regions using standard mobile devices.
details.whyItMatters: NTN extends cellular coverage to the 90 percent of Earth's surface without cell towers. It enables global smartphone connectivity without specialized satellite phones for the first time.
takeaways: 3GPP standards integrate satellites into the 5G architecture
Standard smartphones can connect to NTN satellites directly
HAPS provide coverage from the stratosphere for large areas

faq.question: Can regular phones connect to satellites?
faq.answer: Yes — 3GPP Release 17 enables direct satellite connectivity for standard smartphones. Apple's Emergency SOS via satellite and T-Mobile's Starlink direct-to-cell service demonstrate this. Initial services offer text messaging, with voice and data planned as satellite capabilities increase.

faq.question: What are high-altitude platform stations?
faq.answer: HAPS are solar-powered aircraft or balloons operating at 20 kilometers altitude in the stratosphere. They provide cellular coverage over areas of 100 kilometers or more, filling the gap between terrestrial towers and orbital satellites. They are easier to deploy and update than satellites.
